This is a topic I've come back to all my life really, but particularly in the past few years, since I came to a notably eye-opening realization.

I'll start with the realization and get it out there in its bare form, then work around it.

-----

There is only one thing that any person can actually DO to promote "rights" or "freedom," and that is to *extend them to other people*.

-----

I've found that the easiest way to explain this is by way of a thought exercise:

1. Bob and Tom are on a desert island.

2. Bob insist that he, Bob, possesses a right to life.

3. Does Bob then, for all practical purposes, actually possess a right to life?

or

1. Bob and Tom are on a desert island.

2. *Tom* insists that Bob possesses a right to life.

3. Does Bob then, for all practical purposes, possess a right to life?

-----

It doesn't (or at least shouldn't) take long to recognize the truth here. In the first case - the case in which Bob insists that he himself possesses a right to life, he in fact, for all practical purposes, does not actually possess such a right, since Tom can simply choose to deny him that right and kill him, and his purported right can do absolutely nothing to stop that.

But the first case illustrates how most individuals approach the idea of rights (and of freedom). In the best case, they simply proclaim that they possess that "right" and carry on, as if it's some sort of incantation that alters reality, and in worse (and much more common) cases, they set about attempting to ensure that "right," most often by at least threatening if not actively undermining the rights and freedoms of other people, and thus threatening if not actively undermining the very concept of "rights" and "freedom."

But in the second case, Bob really does, simply by Tom's action, possess a full and measurable "right to life." Just by the fact that Tom has recognized such a right AND EXTENDED IT TO BOB, Bob in fact possesses that which is otherwise merely a long-sought ideal. He really does, and immediately, possess the magic shield society has so long pursued - he can go about his life, safe in the knowledge that he possesses a right to do so and that that right will not be violated, and all simply because TOM extended it to him. And if he also extends to Tom the right to life, then instantly we have the ideal made real - a civilization in which all really do, and absolutely, possess a right to life.

It must be noted that application of this awareness throughout a society appears, at least so far in our history, to be an impossibility.

But still...
I think the right to life thing involves intercession by third parties.

I don't. In fact, I would go so far as to say that intercession by third parties destroys rights by turning them into privileges, and is in fact the worst way to attempt to protect rights.

Chief among the problems is that most attempts to protect rights boil down to selectively denying rights. This is the other side of the coin I outlined in the first post.

In the most extreme and simplest case - if I believe that you pose a threat to my life - if, for instance, you aim a gun at my head and say that you're going to shoot me, and I respond by shooting and killing you, then I have explicitly negated your right to life.

Lots of arguments are made surrounding that - that the person who issues the threat gives up his rights by doing so or whatever - and I don't intend to get into those here. The simple fact is that, whether nominally justified or not, my response to your purported threat to my life - to your apparent intention to deny my right to life - was to deny your right to life. That's... problematic, at least.

When one introduces a third party to the dynamic, it simply becomes even more problematic, since that third party must be seen to possess the authority necessary to deny the rights of the person posing the threat. It's no longer even as simple as you putting a gun to my head and me killing you - violating your right to your life - in order to end your threat to my right to my life. Now it's some third party who intercedes. The only way that that's even practical is if the third party is proactively seen to possess the authority to do so, and if that's the case, then that means, of necessity, that that third party possesses the authority to deny rights. As soon as that's the case, they're no longer actually "rights" at all, since they can be denied by the authority of the third party. They are in fact now mere privileges, since they can be granted and revoked, merely as whoever possesses the authority decrees.

As I said earlier, all of this comes from the other side of the coin I outlined in my first post - the negative approach to the issue, so to speak. Not only do rights not exist unless they're extended by individuals to other individuals, but rights cannot exist so long as anyone is seen to possess sufficient authority to deny them, since the mere fact that someone possesses the authority to deny them makes them privileges rather than rights.
